note: Every figure was read from its primary source on the date in 'checked'. Re-check when a source publishes a newer release.

unites.source: Program for Public Consultation, University of Maryland
unites.title: The National Common Ground
unites.sample: 2,509 U.S. adults (each question asked of four of five random subsamples, about 2,000 people)
unites.method: Online opt-in panels (Cint, Dynata, Prodege), weighted by age, race, ethnicity, gender, education, income, region, home ownership and party. Margin of error ±2.9 points. Response rate 7.6%.

misread.finding: We underestimate how varied the other side is.
misread.detail: Democrats and Republicans underestimated the range of views inside both parties by more than a factor of two. They did not measurably overestimate how extreme the average member of the other party is. People who saw more variety in the other party liked it more and worried less about it.
misread.source: Dias, Lelkes and Pearl, Annenberg School for Communication, University of Pennsylvania. Political Science Research and Methods

misread.finding: Most of our disagreement is real.
misread.detail: Democrats and Republicans made similar mistakes about both parties, and disliking the other party did not make people see it as more uniformly extreme. The researchers' conclusion: “real disagreements, not necessarily misperceptions.”
misread.source: Huber and Orr, Yale ISPS. Frontiers in Political Science
misread.sample: YouGov surveys of 5,000+ adults, before the 2020 and 2024 elections

gap.title: The Perception Gap
gap.method: Each person said whether they agreed with seven statements, then guessed, from 0 to 100, what share of the other party agreed. Margin of error ±2.1 points.
